Apple has officially launched the Apple Upgrade leasing program today, operating much as外界 had anticipated. Although the program makes products more affordable through monthly installments, users face the risk of being trapped in an endless cycle of leases.

The reason is that this program does not completely replace the iPhone Upgrade Program — after the lease term ends, users will not actually own the device……

As Apple product prices reach all-time highs, it is undeniable that lowering monthly payments to make products more accessible does hold a certain appeal. When it comes to monthly installments alone, the Apple Upgrade program certainly achieves this.

For example, you can lease a MacBook Pro equipped with 16GB of memory and 1TB of storage for as little as US$38.99 per month. This model enables more Apple devices to reach more consumers, which is undoubtedly a good thing.

Concerns about the Apple Upgrade program

However, the worry is exactly what I predicted last week: people will treat this program exactly like car leasing. Although you have the option to pay a lump sum at the end of the lease term to take ownership of the car, almost nobody does this. Most car lessees simply return the vehicle and lease a new one, going round and round in circles.

The same situation could arise with the Apple Upgrade program. To fully own the device, you must pay a final lump-sum amount equal to the difference between the total rent you have already paid and the device's original retail price.

Let's do a calculation using the MacBook Pro mentioned above (amounts rounded to the nearest whole number):

36-month plan

  • Monthly payment: US$38.99
  • Total amount paid: US$1,403
  • Lump sum required to obtain ownership of the device: US$585

24-month plan

  • Monthly payment: US$53.99
  • Total amount paid: US$1,295
  • Lump sum required to obtain ownership of the device: US$703

For those who cannot afford to buy the device outright, this sum is by no means a small amount. Unless they have been saving up beforehand, it is very likely they will struggle to come up with the money. When that time comes, the most likely scenario is that they will start a new cycle all over again.

If you can afford it, a more advanced approach is

If you can afford higher monthly payments, a smarter approach is to create your own version of the IUP.

You pay Apple the monthly lease as usual, while at the same time setting aside an additional amount each month into a savings account to pay the lump sum at the end of the lease term. Taking the 36-month MBP lease as an example, the figures would be roughly as follows:

  • Monthly lease payment: US$38.99
  • Monthly savings contribution: US$16.26
  • Total monthly outlay: US$55.25
  • Total paid to Apple: US$1,403
  • Total amount saved toward the lump sum: US$585.36 (plus any interest earned)

igorsky's most-liked comment

This article (along with those self-righteous comments) paints everyone with the same brush. Some of us just like to upgrade to a new phone every year — now it just makes that easier. If you buy a new phone with cash and sell the old one every year, the cost is about the same as leasing a new one. People should stop assuming everyone has the same spending habits.

Then you can use the money you've saved to pay that US$585 lump sum, and the device will be entirely yours.

Of course, if you really want to upgrade to a new device, no one can stop you from selling the one you currently own and signing a new lease. The proceeds from a private resale will very likely be enough to cover the new lump sum — you can simply put that back into your savings account, so that your monthly outlay going forward is just the lease payment itself.

How are you planning to finance your future Apple products? Feel free to share in the comments.
